So are we leaning for or against Fascism?

I think some form of fascism or a "neo-fascist" state is inevitable as it is the de facto replacement for the government of a modern nation-state after the collapse of a democratic republic. The exact details of this can be modulated, of course, but I feel strongly that when Western democracy fully collapses, Fascism will be at the forefront of the revolutionary process.

Other possibilities are a regression to a feudal Monarchism, or a recapitulation of communism. I don't think feudalism can work in a modern, industrial society, but national syndicalism represents a modern 'echo' of the principal. Caesarism is definitely a strong possibility, and there are varied opinions on how closely that maps to a fascist state. Certainly Mussolini saw himself as a modern Caesar, while other important luminaries like Oswald Spengler felt that some form of National Socialism was significantly different and in opposition to Caesarism.

I would think that in practice, a failed state will revert to something like Caesarism, one can see that the Fuhrer-cult of Germany was an expression of this; even though conceptually, national socialism was supposed to be built upon the "blood and soil" of the 'volk', in practice I would suggest that it functioned via a vanguard party with a political aristocracy.

In short, I would say that I believe the collapse of democracy to be inevitable, and that we should strive to replace it with something sustainable and that which gives meaning & purpose to the lives of the people of the nation. If not classical Fascism, some form of synthesis between socialism and fascism should be what we strive for instead of a reversion to totalitarian rule by fiat. A strong central government seems historically inevitable, and I personally have no problem with that. What we should look to ensure is sustainability in our government, which would involve a fusion of traditional society and modern technology, as well as an ideology that fulfills mankind's dual impulses of collective and individual action.

This dual dynamic is very important, and I think we can see the failures of liberalism and communism as being due to a blind focus on one or the other; respectively the former being individualism and the latter being collectivism. Fascism is the only political theory, currently, that addresses both aspects. While I think it is quite possible that we can develop a "fourth political theory" that better addresses contemporary issues and the state of the 'soul' of Western civilization, I feel strongly that this fourth theory will borrow most heavily from the third, fascism, rather than the first two (liberalism and communism). I feel this way because fascism also fully embraces the rational and irrational impulses of the Western mind, and to me seems tailored to our "faustian soul," addressing our American/European cultures specifically rather than attempting to claim universality.

So, I am leaning for Fascism as a bulwark against a completely irrational ideology of rule by divine right where on individual holds a god-like status. In this way I feel that something like a triumvirate or council should make up the executive head of the State. I don;t think that a singular Emperor or Caesar is necessarily dangerous or bad, but I feel strongly that there must exist an ethos that binds the citizens together in common cause, and any titular head must represent this National Will, rather than their own personal designs and whims.

Very well said, and I think you're absolutely correct in pointing out how fascism is especially well tailored to the west's "Faustian soul." In this respect, I would say I am leaning for fascism as well. But I also think this is where fascism reaches its philosophical apex. Although in practice and theory superior to both liberalism and communism, fascism (as it has been interpreted thus far) only reacts to modernity rather than seeking to overcome it. The underlying impulse of fascism is the Nietzschean will to power, which Heidegger (and I think correctly) diagnosed as the culmination of western metaphysics dating back to Plato. I think in this respect national socialism transcends fascism, at least in its orientation to the overall history of western metaphysics. I also think Heidegger was correct in that he saw national socialism as the "event' in the opening up of an entire new epoch in the history of Being.
